topic: Design a chat app: WebSockets, push & message delivery

questions.question: While a chat screen is open, both users send and receive messages many times a minute. Which transport fits best?
options: Short polling the messages endpoint every 2 seconds
A WebSocket kept open while the app is in the foreground
Server-Sent Events for both sending and receiving
Long polling with a new HTTP request for every outgoing message and incoming batch
questions.explanation: A WebSocket is one persistent, full-duplex connection, so the server pushes messages instantly and each frame costs little. Short polling wastes radio and battery on empty responses. Long polling adds a round trip per batch. SSE only goes server to client, so sends would still need separate HTTP calls.

questions.question: On modern Android, a chat app can reliably keep its WebSocket open in the background for hours to receive messages, without a foreground service, as long as it reconnects when the socket drops.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Doze, App Standby and background execution limits cut off network access and can kill the process, so background sockets aren't reliable. They also drain the battery. The standard design is a socket in the foreground and FCM push in the background.

questions.question: The user puts your chat app in the background. Which parts of the design are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Close the WebSocket soon after the app leaves the foreground
Have the server send an FCM message for new messages while the device has no live socket
When the push arrives, sync from the server using the last-seen cursor instead of trusting the push payload alone
Start a foreground service with a permanent notification just to keep the socket alive
Poll the server every minute with a background thread to stay up to date
questions.explanation: Foreground socket plus background push is the standard split, and the push works as a wake-up signal that triggers a cursor-based sync. A foreground service just to hold a socket is the wrong use of one and annoys users. Background polling is battery-hungry and gets throttled by Doze anyway.

questions.question: Before showing a notification, your app must check the local database (is the conversation muted? was the message already read on another device?). Which FCM message type should the server send?
options: A notification message, because the system shows it even when the app is killed
A notification message with a data payload, read in `onMessageReceived` in all cases
A data message, so `onMessageReceived` decides whether and how to notify
A topic message to a topic named after the conversation
questions.explanation: Data messages always go to `onMessageReceived`, so your code runs and can check Room before building (or skipping) the notification. When the app is in the background, a notification message (even one with data) is shown straight in the tray by the system and `onMessageReceived` isn't called, so you can't apply this logic.

questions.question: Each outgoing message gets a UUID generated on the device before it's sent. What is the main reason?
options: So retries are idempotent and the server can drop duplicates
So messages can be ordered by UUID in the conversation
So the server doesn't need to store its own id for the message
So the message is encrypted with the UUID as its key
questions.explanation: If the ack is lost and the client retries, the server sees the same client id and returns the existing message instead of storing it twice. The client can also match the server's echo to its local row. Random UUIDs carry no order, so they can't be used for sorting.

questions.question: FCM delivers every message exactly once and in order, so the app can insert each push payload into Room and skip syncing with the server.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: FCM is best-effort. Messages can be delayed, collapsed, dropped (for example after too many pending messages or a long time offline) or arrive out of order. Treat a push as a 'something changed, go sync' signal and fetch from the server using your cursor.

questions.question: Messages in a conversation are sorted by the sender device's `System.currentTimeMillis()`. Users report replies showing up above the message they answer. What's the best fix?
options: Sort by the receiving device's clock instead, since it sees the real order
Sort by a server-assigned per-conversation sequence number
Sync every device's clock with NTP before sending
Sort by the client-generated UUID
questions.explanation: Device clocks drift and can be set wrong, so timestamps from different senders can't be compared. A per-conversation sequence assigned by the server gives one order that every client agrees on. The receiver's clock only records arrival order, and you can't make every client keep an accurate clock.

questions.question: The phone was in a tunnel for 10 minutes. The WebSocket reconnects. How should the client get the messages it missed?
options: Reload the latest 50 messages and replace the local list
Ask for messages sent after the device's local time when the socket dropped
Page from the last sequence number stored locally
Wait for the server to replay missed messages over the new socket
questions.explanation: A last-seen sequence cursor is exact: nothing is skipped or fetched twice, however long the gap. The latest 50 can leave holes after a long gap. A local-time cutoff runs into clock skew. A plain socket has no replay unless you build one, and that's the same cursor logic anyway.

questions.question: A chat server deploy drops 2 million WebSocket connections at once. Which client reconnect behaviours stop the clients from overloading the servers when they come back? Select all that apply.
options: Exponential backoff between reconnect attempts
Random jitter added to each backoff delay
A maximum cap on the backoff delay
Retrying every second on a fixed timer until the connection works
Retrying immediately in a tight loop so users see messages as soon as possible
questions.explanation: Without jitter, clients that disconnected together retry together and keep hitting the servers in synchronized waves (the thundering herd). Exponential backoff spreads out the load as failures continue, jitter breaks up the waves, and the cap keeps a user from waiting forever. Fixed or immediate retries keep the herd synchronized.

questions.question: A message moves through sending → sent → delivered → read. What should flip it from 'sending' to 'sent'?
options: The send call on the WebSocket returning without an error
The recipient's device confirming it received the message
The server's ack that it stored the message
The recipient opening the conversation
questions.explanation: 'Sent' means the server has the message for sure, which only its ack (usually carrying its server id and sequence number) proves. A successful local write only means the bytes went into a buffer, and the connection may die before they arrive. The recipient's device confirming is 'delivered', and the recipient opening the conversation is 'read'.

questions.question: The app shows 'connected', but no messages have arrived for 5 minutes. Server logs show the server closed the connection long ago. What should the client add?
options: A bigger socket read buffer so frames aren't dropped
Ping/pong heartbeats with a reconnect on timeout
An FCM message every 30 seconds to keep the app awake
A longer connect timeout on the OkHttp client
questions.explanation: Mobile NATs and carrier proxies silently drop idle connections, which leaves a half-open socket that looks fine on the client. Heartbeats keep the NAT mapping alive and detect dead connections quickly. Pick the interval as a trade-off between how fast you detect drops and how often you wake the radio.

questions.question: Typing indicators and online presence should be stored in Room and synced reliably, just like messages.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Typing and presence are ephemeral: they only matter right now, so they're sent over the live socket, fire-and-forget, and expire on a timer. Storing and replaying them would show 'typing...' from an hour ago and waste storage and bandwidth.

questions.question: Some conversations have 50,000 messages. How should the chat screen load history?
options: Load every message from Room into a `List` in the ViewModel when the screen opens
Page from Room by sequence number, fetching older pages via a `before_seq` cursor
Always load history straight from the network with `?page=N` offsets and skip the database
Load the newest 100 messages and stop the user from scrolling further back
questions.explanation: Paging 3 over Room keeps memory bounded and works offline, and a RemoteMediator with a sequence cursor fills older gaps. Loading everything wastes memory and slows startup. Offset pages shift as new messages arrive, which causes duplicates or skipped messages. Capping history is a product regression, not a design.

questions.question: The user sends a message while in airplane mode. What should happen?
options: Show an error and clear the input field
Disable the send button until the network comes back
Keep the message only in ViewModel memory and send it when the socket reconnects
Save it in Room as 'pending' and send it from a WorkManager outbox
questions.explanation: A persistent outbox makes the message survive process death and appear immediately (local echo), and it's retried automatically, e.g. by WorkManager with a network constraint. Keeping it only in memory loses it if the app is killed. Errors or a disabled send button break the offline-first experience users expect from chat.

questions.question: Users can send 200 MB videos. Which parts of the design are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Upload the file to blob storage separately (for example to a pre-signed URL), then send a chat message that references the media id
Use a resumable or chunked upload so a dropped connection doesn't restart the whole upload
Include a small thumbnail or blur placeholder and the dimensions in the message so recipients can lay it out before downloading
Base64-encode the video and send it as a WebSocket frame so it arrives in order with the text
Have recipients download the full video automatically on any network so it plays instantly
questions.explanation: Separating media upload from the message keeps the socket free for small, real-time frames, and resumable uploads survive flaky mobile networks. Base64 makes the payload about 33% bigger and blocks the socket. Auto-downloading big files on mobile data burns the user's data plan, so most apps download on Wi-Fi only or on tap.

questions.question: The chat is end-to-end encrypted. Product asks for 'search all my messages'. How does this have to work?
options: Index messages on the server in Elasticsearch when they arrive
Send the search query to the server, which decrypts matching conversations
Store a plaintext copy on the server just for search
Search on the device, e.g. a Room FTS table
questions.explanation: With E2EE the private keys live only on devices, so the server only sees ciphertext and can't index or decrypt it. Any server-side option breaks the encryption promise. The index is built from the decrypted messages stored locally. The trade-off is that search only covers history that's on the device.

questions.question: The app inserts a sent message into Room right away (local echo). The server then pushes the same message back over the socket with its server id and sequence number, and users see it twice. What's the right fix?
options: Skip the local insert and wait for the server echo
Upsert the echo into the existing row by client message id
Ignore every incoming socket message whose sender is the current user
Remove duplicates in the UI by comparing message text and timestamp
questions.explanation: The client-generated id is the shared key between the optimistic row and the server's copy, so a unique index on it plus an upsert that fills in server id, sequence and 'sent' state turns the echo into a state update. Waiting for the echo makes sending feel slow and breaks offline sends. Ignoring your own messages loses the ones you sent from another device. Matching on text and time breaks when you send identical texts.

questions.question: It's fine to send every chat event (read receipts, presence changes, typing) as a high-priority FCM message so the app always gets them immediately.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: High priority is meant for messages that lead to a user-visible notification. Android can downgrade an app's high-priority messages to normal if they keep not producing notifications. Send background events as normal priority or let them catch up on the next sync.

questions.question: You add groups of up to 5,000 members (no end-to-end encryption). Which choices on the client side are sound? Select all that apply.
options: The client uploads the message once and the server fans it out to members
Show combined read status (for example 'Read by 312') instead of tracking delivery ticks for every member
Get presence and typing only for members who are currently visible or active, not the whole group
The client sends a separate copy to each member to make sure every member gets it
Open a separate WebSocket for each group the user is in
questions.explanation: Fan-out belongs on the server, since one upload from a phone is far cheaper than 5,000. Per-member receipts and presence for big groups mean too many events and too much UI, so they're combined or limited to who's visible. One multiplexed socket carries all conversations, and a socket per group multiplies the connection and battery cost.

questions.question: Several friends message the user while the app is closed. Which notification behaviours make sense for a chat app? Select all that apply.
options: Group notifications per conversation (for example with `MessagingStyle`) and add new messages to the existing one
Offer inline reply with `RemoteInput`, sending the reply through the same outbox
Clear or update the notification when the conversation is read on another device
Post a new separate notification for every single message
Make the reply action always open the full app before sending
questions.explanation: Grouping per conversation keeps the notification shade readable, and inline reply lets users answer without opening the app. Using the outbox means the reply is retried like any other message. A notification per message floods the shade. A read sync should clear stale notifications so users aren't nagged about messages they've already seen.
